QF.id: SIA Assessment Frameworks Techniques and Standards_26

question.text: For a binary outcome with expected proportion p=0.5 (most conservative), 95% confidence level (z=1.96), and desired margin of error e=5%, the minimum sample size from an infinite population is closest to:

explanation.text: The Logic: The standard sample-size formula for estimating a proportion from a large/infinite population is n = z² x p x (1-p) / e². For a 95% confidence level z = 1.96; for the most conservative variability assumption p = 0.5 (which maximises p x (1-p) = 0.25); and for a desired margin of error e = 5% = 0.05. Substituting: n = (1.96)² x 0.5 x 0.5 / (0.05)² = 3.8416 x 0.25 / 0.0025 = 0.9604 / 0.0025 = 384.16, which rounds up to 385. This is the classic n ≈ 385 benchmark used in survey and beneficiary sampling. The Trap: 96 drops the z² multiplier from the numerator. 196 results from arithmetic confusion around the z² term. 1,067 corresponds to the same formula with e = 3% instead of 5% (tighter precision quadruples-ish the sample). Only 385 matches the stated inputs z = 1.96, p = 0.5, e = 5%. Note: The cited workbook pages (124, 131 of the Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook) mention the need for an appropriate sample size and state that statistically significant sample sizes require defining a confidence interval and a margin of error, but they do not present the n = z²·p·(1-p)/e² formula or the 385 benchmark. The framing above reflects standard statistics/survey-methodology practice used widely in social-research and audit-sampling.
